text.p: American swimmer Jessica Foschi had her two-year suspension for steroid use cut by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Wednesday, clearing the way for her immediate return to international competition.

FINA, international swimming's governing body, who had banned Foschi after she tested positive for the metabolic steroid nesteroton at the 1995 U.S. national championships and who later turned down an appeal, were ordered to pay the American teenager 15,000 Swiss francs to cover her court costs.
"We respect the decision of the court," said FINA executive director Cornel Marculescu. "The decision of the court is final.
"We don't know the reasons for the decision, just the decision that was made."
The CAS reduced the suspension from two years to six months, from August 4 1995 to February 3 1996.

In making the ruling, the CAS acknowledged that Foschi had committed an offence under FINA medical rules which say that the identification of a banned substance or any of its metabolites in a competitor's urine can result in two-year suspension.
"I'm puzzled by the decision," said FINA counsel Jean-Pierre Morand. "They (CAS) acknowledged a positive test and that an offence had been committed.
"Why they chose to reduce it to nothing, I have no idea. That information will be forthcoming in the next months."
The ruling ends a rollercoaster saga of bans and appeals that stretches back to August 4 1995 when the then 15-year-old American first tested positive.

Foschi, who has steadfastly maintained her innocence and claimed the tests were sabotaged, was originally placed on two years' probation last June by the U.S. Swimming National Board of Review but a subsequent appeal to the American Arbitration Association reversed all sanctions.
Under growing pressure to clean up the sport, FINA took up the case and conducted their own investigation suspending the swimmer for two years on August 3 1996.
"The evidence showed that FINA's due process is a travesty," said Foschi's lawyer Mark Levinstein. "They don't know their own rules.
"The rules are so badly written, who knows what they mean? They just have this concept that they can do as they please."
